title: Count Triplets with Even XOR Set Bits I
statement:
You are given three integer arrays `a`, `b` and `c`. A triplet picks one element from each array, `(a[i], b[j], c[k])`, for any indices `i`, `j` and `k`. Triplets are told apart by their indices, so equal values at different positions make different triplets.

Return how many triplets have the property that `a[i] XOR b[j] XOR c[k]` has an **even** number of `1` bits in binary. A XOR of `0` has zero `1` bits, which counts as even.
signature: int tripletCount(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c)
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way tries all `a.length * b.length * c.length` triplets, XORs each one and counts its bits: up to a million checks here. A faster view rests on one fact: `ones(x XOR y) = ones(x) + ones(y) - 2 * ones(x AND y)`, because a bit set in both numbers vanishes from the XOR. Subtracting an even amount never changes evenness, so the XOR of a triplet has an even bit count exactly when the bit counts of its three values add up to an even number. Only each value's **parity** (even or odd number of `1` bits) matters.

## Approach

1. For each array, tally the values with an even number of `1` bits (`counts[0]`) and with an odd number (`counts[1]`); the bit loop flips `parity` once for every `1` it shifts out of `rest`. This gives `countA`, `countB` and `countC`.
2. Enumerate the parity `p` of the element from `a` and `q` of the element from `b`. The element from `c` must then have parity `p ^ q`, so that the three parities sum to an even number.
3. Every such choice of three elements is a good triplet, so add `countA[p] * countB[q] * countC[p ^ q]` to `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`a = [1]`, `b = [2]`, `c = [3]`. In binary 1 is `1` and 2 is `10` (one bit each, odd), while 3 is `11` (two bits, even). So `countA = [0, 1]`, `countB = [0, 1]` and `countC = [1, 0]`. Of the four `(p, q)` pairs only `p = 1, q = 1` has elements in both `a` and `b`; it needs parity `1 ^ 1 = 0` from `c`, adding `1 * 1 * 1 = 1`. The answer is `1`, matching `1 XOR 2 XOR 3 = 0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(a.length + b.length + c.length): each value takes at most 7 bit steps (values are at most 100), then 4 products.
- Space: O(1): three pairs of counters.

## Pitfalls

- A XOR of `0` has zero `1` bits, which is even, so that triplet counts.
- Triplets are counted by position: equal values in one array each count (Example 2 counts both `1`s of `a`).
- Only parities combine simply: `ones(x XOR y)` is usually not `ones(x) + ones(y)`, but it always has the same evenness.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `countParities` | helper returning `[even, odd]` bit-count tallies for one array |
| `parity`, `rest` | running bit-count parity of `value`, and the bits of `value` not yet read |
| `countA`, `countB`, `countC` | the tallies for `a`, `b` and `c` |
| `p`, `q` | parities chosen for the elements from `a` and `b` |
| `total` | number of good triplets found so far |
